cvEn:
Alexei Blitzki, son of Ludmila and Alexander, was born on 15 Elul 5741 (14 September 1981) in the city of Ryazan, Russia. He has a brother, Boris.

Alexei was a shy, gentle and courteous child. He received his first education in a kindergarten in his city and continued to primary school there. From the age of eight until eleven he lived with his family in Czechoslovakia, where his father worked on an overseas posting. At the age of twelve he returned to Ryazan to continue his studies there.

In 1996 the family immigrated to Israel and settled in Rishon LeZion. Alexei entered the "Dorot" primary school and, despite his shyness, was warmly welcomed by the children of his class. He completed his secondary education at the Kerry Real Gymnasium in the city. He was not one of the outstanding students, but he finished his studies successfully. In his spare time he worked and saved money.

Alexei developed a deep interest in culture and the arts. He loved literature, poetry, cinema and theater, read many books in both Russian and Hebrew, and was a great admirer of Israel's major playwright, Hanoch Levin. He knew Israeli cinema well and was especially fond of the films "Alex Is in Love" by Boaz Davidson, one of the great cult films of all time, "Circus Palestina" by Eyal Halfon, and "Yana's Friends" by Arik Kaplan, and he tried to pass this love on to his family. In the graduation yearbook of the Real Gymnasium, the following was written about him: "Alexei Blitzki – Record: closing doors. Medical problem: excessive niceness. Film: 'Alex Is in Love.' Obsession: changing the class. Message from the class: live and let live."

With his quiet nature, Alexei gathered friends around him who knew how to appreciate his good heart, his spiritual richness and the compassion he showed toward the weak. Alexei had a well-developed social and political consciousness and held firm opinions. As a teenager he joined the Meretz youth movement, where he found partners who shared his views and principles, became an active and engaged member of the movement, and made good friends.

Although he was a devoted pacifist, as his conscription drew near Alexei said, "I owe a debt to the state that took us in." He was drafted into the IDF on 31 July 2000, was posted to the Armored Corps, and served as a radio operator in the 195th Battalion, "Adam."

In the army Alexei met new friends who became soulmates, and he spent his free time with them. He smiled and laughed often, and felt the camaraderie and pride of his unit.

His service was not an easy one. The events of the "Tide and Ebb" period and the terror attacks that claimed the lives of hundreds of Israelis posed many challenges for his unit, and he took part in many operations. Among others, he participated in Operation "Defensive Shield," which the IDF carried out in the spring of 2002 in Judea and Samaria. Alexei did not often get home, but during the short leaves he received he shared his experiences with his parents, and he insisted on translating every military term into Russian for them. "He felt very Israeli. It was important to him to make that integration," his mother related. Alexei also kept his friends in Russia updated on his new life, and described his feelings in letters he wrote: "... I believe you have heard of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and the terror attacks that take place here. Unfortunately, my unit also takes part in preventing these acts; more than once I have been at a checkpoint or in a tank when we were fired upon, and of course we had to return fire. ... Service here is basically not completely safe, but there is nothing to be done. I live in a country like this, although I would have preferred that peace reign here. If you see a news report about Israeli tanks, it is quite likely that I am in one of them at that moment. I know there was a report about our tanks on Russian news about half a year ago, in the summer, when we surrounded the Palestinian city of Jenin. My crew and I were inside the tank for three days without being able to get out."

In another letter he wrote: "For the last four months we have been holding a position near Bethlehem, and we will be here for another two months. After that we go out for training, and after that we will hold a position in the Golan Heights. Although the service is not easy and not the safest, I love it. I have made many friends in the army, and we are very close, which helps us get through the daily difficulties."

Alexei was due to be discharged from the IDF within five months, and he was already planning his next step: nursing studies at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, a profession that suited his character and personality. In his last conversation with his mother, held on Friday evening, Alexei said he was due to go on leave at the beginning of the week, and remarked that he was troubled that he was leaving while his friends stayed in the Gaza Strip. A few hours later, his life was cut short.

Alexei fell in an operational activity near Dugit on 13 Adar I 5763 (15 February 2003). Alexei and his fellow crew members were making their way to one of the posts in northern Gaza when the tank struck a charge weighing about one hundred kilograms. The fire that broke out as a result of the explosion caused the ammunition in the tank to ignite and explode as well, and all the tank's occupants were killed on the spot. Alongside Alexei fell Staff Sergeant Doron Cohen, his close friend, Staff Sergeant Itai Mizrahi, and Sergeant Noam Behagon.

The muddy ground in the area of the explosion prevented fire trucks from reaching the site. Only after the ammunition stopped exploding were the firefighters able to put out the fire with hand extinguishers, and the damaged tank was towed with the help of bulldozers to the nearby community of Dugit. Another two hours passed before the bodies of the soldiers were extracted. An additional charge was later discovered in the area of the incident and was neutralized by combat engineers.

Alexei, twenty-one years old at his death, was laid to rest in the military cemetery in Rishon LeZion. He left behind his parents and a brother, who is also a soldier. After his death he was posthumously promoted to the rank of Sergeant First Class.
